title: Structure-Preserving Quantum Simulation of Wave Equations on a Trapped-Ion Processor
authors: Abhishek Shringi, Hsuan-Cheng Wu, Ahmed Shokry, Xiantao Li, Mahmut Taylan Kandemir
abstract: Wave equations provide a natural testbed for near-term quantum simulation of partial differential equations, but hardware demonstrations have remained limited in spatial dimension, equation class, system size, and physically meaningful output. We develop and benchmark structure-preserving, Fourier-based quantum circuits for the one- and two dimensional acoustic wave equations and Dirac dynamics with variable mass on the Quantinuum H2-2 trapped-ion processor. The experiments include one-dimensional grids with up to \(1024\) points and \(32\times32\) two-dimensional grids, corresponding to an encoded state-space dimension of up to \(4096\). Rather than reconstructing the full fields, we estimate subdomain kinetic energies directly from measurement samples. Across all tested acoustic and Dirac dynamics problems, the H2-2 results track the classical kinetic-energy dynamics with mean absolute errors between \(5.9\times10^{-3}\) and \(2.4\times10^{-2}\). At fixed retained bandwidth, the compiled gate counts grow approximately quadratically with the number of grid qubits; the acoustic circuit sizes are essentially independent of evolution time, whereas the cost also grows with the number of product-formula steps. These results provide hardware-level evidence that accurate observable dynamics can remain resolvable for structured wave problems with thousands of encoded degrees of freedom on a present-day trapped-ion processor.
summary: The paper presents the development and benchmarking of structure-preserving quantum circuits designed to simulate wave equations like the acoustic and Dirac equations. Using the Quantinuum H2-2 trapped-ion processor, they successfully measured observable dynamics on grids up to $32 	imes 32$, showing that accurate simulation is feasible for complex physical systems with thousands of degrees of freedom.
main_problem: The primary goal is developing a quantum simulation method for structure-preserving wave equations (PDEs) on near-term quantum hardware.
main_result: The simulations successfully tracked classical kinetic-energy dynamics for acoustic and Dirac problems on the H2-2 processor with low mean absolute errors, demonstrating feasibility for structured wave problems.
method: The authors developed Fourier-based quantum circuits utilizing techniques like exact bright–dark decomposition (for 2D acoustics) and Strang splitting (for variable mass Dirac dynamics).
model_or_system: The work simulates the one-dimensional acoustic wave equation, two-dimensional acoustic equations, and the variable mass Dirac equation. The experiments were performed on the Quantinuum H2-2 trapped-ion processor.
key_observables: Subdomain kinetic energies (for acoustics) and spinor-component populations (for Dirac dynamics).
important_parameters: Tested up to 1D grids of 1024 points and $32 	imes 32$ 2D grids, corresponding to state-space dimensions up to 4096.
main_assumptions: The results are benchmarked on structured inputs and observable dynamics, not establishing a quantum advantage over classical solvers; the scope is limited to periodic boundary conditions.
figures_summary: Figures detail the overall circuits for 1D and 2D acoustic evolution (using QFTs), gate-level decompositions of propagators, and specific state preparation circuits for initial conditions like cosine or Gaussian profiles.
paper_structure: The paper details the formulation of wave equations into quantum Hamiltonians, presents the structure-preserving circuit design using Fourier methods, benchmarks these circuits on the H2-2 processor across different dimensions/equations, and analyzes resource scaling.
why_interesting: This work directly applies advanced quantum simulation techniques to fundamental PDEs (wave dynamics) using a state-of-the-art trapped-ion platform, providing concrete hardware evidence for simulating continuous physical systems beyond simple qubit registers.

Solid curves show the logical circuit before hardware-native compilation; markers show the circuit compiled for the Quantinuum H2-2 native gate set using H2-2E, with dashed curves denoting least-squares fits. Blue denotes total gate count or depth, and orange denotes the corresponding two-qubit contribution. (a),(c) Gate count and circuit depth, respectively, as functions of t ∈[0, 1] at fixed nh = 10. (b),(d) Gate count and circuit depth as functions of the number nh of grid qubits at fixed t = 0.1.

FIG. 3. Half-domain kinetic energy for the one-dimensional cosine pressure initial state with k0 = 1 on a grid of Nh = 1024 points (nh = 10 grid qubits and 11 qubits in total). (a) The classical reference trajectory is compared with noiseless finite-shot AerSimulator results, the H2-2E noise-modeled emulator, and measurements from the Quantin- uum H2-2 processor. (b) Absolute error |⟨KE⟩method −⟨KE⟩classical| at each sampled time. A dash denotes a time not sampled on the corresponding backend. The mean absolute errors are 3.7 × 10−3, 1.2 × 10−2, and 1.1 × 10−2 for AerSimulator, H2-2E, and H2-2, respectively.
